storm.summary_layperson: No storms are on radar anywhere near the cove, the atmosphere has essentially no instability to work with (CAPE near 0), and there are no watches or warnings in effect through the evening.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer is standing tonight — the air is already about 2°F cooler than the Sound, the opposite of the setup needed for a protective layer — but it's moot since nothing is approaching to blunt.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar shows no echoes in the region and there are no active NWS alerts. The HRRR sounding has CAPE pinned at 0 J/kg through the entire forecast window, and the latest OKX area forecast discussion explicitly calls instability chances "very low to none" — there's no fuel for storms to develop locally, and nothing organized is tracking in from outside the area either.

The cove's usual defense against storms that do arrive — a stable marine layer formed when cool Sound water sits under warmer air — isn't available tonight, but not because it's weak; the setup is inverted. Water (74°F) is actually running about 2°F warmer than the air (72°F) at fetch time, and the trend model shows that gap staying negative (air cooler than water) for the rest of the evening as air temperatures fall further after sunset. A protective layer needs the air to be the warmer side of that gap by roughly 5°F or more; that condition isn't close to being met.

None of this matters much tonight specifically because there's nothing inbound to blunt or amplify. The cove and the surrounding towns are in the same boat: clear, calm, low-risk evening.

What would change the call: any new HRRR cycle showing CAPE building overnight, a radar echo appearing to the west or northwest, or an NWS watch/advisory being issued. None of those are currently in play.

wind.tactics_blurb: This is a gradient-only evening — the sea-breeze gate isn't close to met (air is 2°F cooler than the Sound, not 5°F warmer), so what you get is puffy NNW gradient flow easing from around 8 kt at 5 PM down to a light 5 kt by mid-evening. wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a moderate gradient-wind evening with no sea breeze in play, not a thermal day (internal code B-moderate). The sea-breeze gate needs both a 5°F+ air-water temperature gap and a favorable gradient; the gap here is actually negative (air about 2°F cooler than the Sound), and 0% of coastal stations show a southerly onshore component — there's no thermal circulation trying to build. The gradient proxy (mean authoritative station speed, 10.9 kt) puts this squarely in the moderate-gradient bucket.

Direction is NNW throughout the window, per the cove geography table that's an offshore-over-land flow: expect it puffy and shifty with oscillations in the 15–30° range rather than clean pressure. RYC is currently reading N at 9° (10-min avg 12 kt, gusting 21), close enough to the HRRR forecast track (335–354° across the window) that there's no meaningful station/model conflict — model and obs converge as the window progresses.

With N–NW flow there's no single favored shore; the best average pressure tends to sit mid-cove, away from the lee of trees and houses along both banks, with big puffs rolling off the NW shore and holes in between. Play the shifts and puffs rather than committing to one side.

Speed trends down through the window: roughly 8 kt with 12 kt gusts at 5 PM, easing to a light 5 kt with 8–9 kt gusts by mid-evening as the gradient wind naturally softens and the boundary layer stabilizes after dark (sunset 7:04 PM). This isn't a thermal collapse — gradient wind doesn't care about the sun — it's a genuine synoptic easing trend in the HRRR run. Fleet impact: 8 kt with gusts to 12 is solid one-design racing early; by 8–9 PM it's drifting into light/finicky territory, still raceable but fleet-dependent.
